summary: Defines a new IMAP untagged response code, INPROGRESS, that reports progress on long-running commands.

plainLanguage.summary: When a server takes a long time, you wonder if it froze. This lets it say how far along it is, like a progress bar.

questions: what is the imap inprogress response code
subtitle: A standard way for an IMAP server to tell a client how far along a slow command is, or just that it is still alive.

tldr.problem: Some IMAP commands take a long time, and the client gets no standard sign of progress. A free-form untagged message like "Still on it, 57% done" works, but nothing about it is consistent.
tldr.mechanism: The server adds an INPROGRESS response code inside untagged OK replies, optionally carrying the command tag, a PROGRESS count and a GOAL count. Servers advertise support with an INPROGRESS capability.
tldr.outcome: Clients can show real progress or simply avoid timing out and dropping the connection. The notifications are only hints about progress and must not be used as authoritative data.

today: RFC 9585 is a Proposed Standard from May 2024 and has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the INPROGRESS response code. It builds on RFC 9051.

sections.title: Why Progress Notifications
sections.content:
IMAP commands, as defined in RFC 9051, can take a considerable time for the server to finish. During that time the client has no information about how things are going. A server can already send a generic untagged reply saying something like "Still on it, 57% done", but that gives no standard way to talk to the client about long-running work.

RFC 9585 adds two things to IMAP: a new INPROGRESS response code, in the style of RFC 5530, and a new INPROGRESS capability that tells the client the server sends such notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine asking a librarian for a huge pile of books and then hearing nothing. This gives the librarian a standard way to call out 'I am halfway there'.

sections.title: Advertising the Capability
sections.content:
A server that supports the extension MUST include INPROGRESS in its response to the CAPABILITY command. That is how a client learns that progress notifications may arrive.

Sending them is still optional for the server. Section 4 says the server MAY send the response code, and the notifications MAY be sent for any IMAP command.
sections.plainLanguage: The server puts a sign on its door saying 'I give progress updates', so visitors know what to expect.

sections.title: The INPROGRESS Response Code
sections.content:
The response code is meant to appear inside an untagged OK reply. It MUST NOT appear in a tagged response, because a tagged response means the command has already finished and further progress notices make no sense.

The code MAY carry a list of three details, in this order:

  • CMD-TAG: the tag of the long-running command. If the tag is not available or contains the ] character, it MUST be NIL.
  • PROGRESS: how many items have been processed so far. It MUST be non-negative and SHOULD only increase. If it is not available, both PROGRESS and GOAL MUST be NIL.
  • GOAL: the total number of items to process. It MUST be positive, MUST be greater than PROGRESS, and SHOULD NOT change between notifications for the same tag. If it is unknown it MUST be NIL.

If the code carries no list at all, every detail is read as NIL. The RFC lists four degrees of completeness: a bare keepalive, a keepalive with the command tag, a progress count with unknown goal, and a progress count with a known goal.
sections.plainLanguage: An update can say which job it is about, how many items are done, and how many there are in total. Any of those can be left as 'I do not know'.

sections.title: How Servers and Clients Should Behave
sections.content:
If a server chooses to send notifications, it is RECOMMENDED to do so every 10 to 15 seconds. They can report progress or simply keep the client from timing out and closing the connection. A command that finishes before the first notification is due produces none, so the client MUST assume PROGRESS is 0 and GOAL is unknown until a notification arrives.

PROGRESS and GOAL SHOULD be counts of the items being processed, usually messages. If that is not possible they SHOULD be percentages, with GOAL set to 100 and PROGRESS between 0 and 99. A server SHOULD NOT send a notification where PROGRESS equals GOAL, since the tagged response should be sent instead.

Servers cannot always keep GOAL constant or PROGRESS increasing, so clients MUST be ready for that. When GOAL changes or PROGRESS goes backward, the recommended reading is that the previous goal was reached but the server found more long-running work to do.

A client MAY ignore the notifications entirely, and decides what to show in any user interface. It MUST NOT treat the values as authoritative for anything except judging progress. For example, it must not use GOAL in place of the real output of a SEARCH to learn how many messages are in a folder.
sections.plainLanguage: The server pipes up every ten to fifteen seconds. The numbers are only a rough guide, like a progress bar, so you should not rely on them for anything else.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The grammar uses ABNF and builds on the IMAP grammar from RFC 9051. The tag is a quoted string or NIL. The state is one of three shapes: both values NIL, a number and NIL (counting with no known goal), or a number and a non-zero number (known goal). The code is the string INPROGRESS optionally followed by a parenthesized tag and state.

Token strings are case-insensitive, and implementations MUST accept them in a case-insensitive way.
sections.plainLanguage: This part is the exact spelling rules, so every server and client writes and reads these messages the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The details are not expected to reveal anything that the command output does not already reveal. The RFC notes that progress details could be worked out anyway by sending a series of commands with different workloads.

The client has to protect itself against a malicious server. It should guard against values that cause arithmetic problems, such as GOAL = 0 or VALUE > GOAL. In those cases the notification MUST be disregarded. Values that are negative or too large to fit in 32 bits cannot occur in a correct implementation of the grammar.
sections.plainLanguage: A client should not trust odd numbers, like a progress bar that says more than 100 percent. It should just ignore those messages.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE FROM THE RFC: A SLOW SEARCH

data.title: Progress during a SEARCH
data.code:
C: A001 search text "this will be slow"
  [13 seconds later]
S: * OK [INPROGRESS ("A001" 454 1000)] Processed 45% of the items
  [14 seconds later]
S: * OK [INPROGRESS ("A001" 999 1000)] Processed 99% of the items
  [5 seconds later]
S: * SEARCH 447 735
S: A001 OK Search completed (23.387 + 0.004 + 0.017 secs).

items.title: CMD-TAG
items.text: Tag of the long-running command, or NIL.

items.title: PROGRESS
items.text: Items processed so far; NIL if unavailable.

items.title: GOAL
items.text: Total items expected; NIL if unknown.
